# Who this document is for

This document describes how authentication works in the `appauth` package, which threats it protects against, which decisions were made and why, and what remains the responsibility of the application. It is written for a developer who is going to add the package to a Shiny app, review the security of an existing app, or work on the package itself. No knowledge of the application the package was originally extracted from is required.

The document describes the **intended behaviour of the package**. Functions are documented individually in the help pages (`?appauth`) and in the other vignettes. For that reason there are no usage examples here, only the design and its rationale.

# What the package does and does not do

**Does (the core, identical in every application):**

* stores passwords only as hashes; plain-text passwords are never accepted;
* login and password sign-in, cookie auto-login, sign-out and forced sign-out;
* brute-force protection (per-login lockout and a global attempt limit);
* blocking and deleting users, with protection against losing the last administrator;
* server-side permission checks (not just hiding buttons in the UI);
* password recovery by email: a one-time link from the email (off by default);
* two-factor authentication (TOTP): optional, a code from an authenticator app plus backup codes (off by default);
* the auth table schema (SQLite, DuckDB, MySQL / MariaDB, PostgreSQL) and its versioned migrations;
* UI modules: sign-in (including the first-administrator creation dialog) and user management.

**Does not (the application or infrastructure is responsible):**

* which permissions exist and which roles can do what (the application defines the permission matrix);
* which actions are logged and where (the package reports events through a hook, and the application does the writing);
* transport protection (HTTPS), proxy settings, server file permissions, secret storage;
* validation of the data the application accepts from the user in its own functions (file names, commands, the application's own SQL);
* sending emails (the email with the recovery link is sent by an application function, for example via `emayili`), creating an OAuth client in the Google Cloud Console, and publishing the app on a domain with HTTPS (sign-in with Google is impossible without a domain).

The boundary follows one principle: *the package contains what must be identical in all applications, because a mistake there creates a vulnerability everywhere; the application contains what legitimately differs.*

# Basic concepts

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| User | a record in the `users` table: login, password hash, role, blocked flag |
| Role | a string from a configurable list (by default `admin`, `user`, `viewer`) |
| Permission | the name of an application feature (for example `Run tasks`) that a role may or may not have |
| Permission source | a function that returns a user's permissions; by default it is built from a "permission -> roles" matrix |
| Administrator | a user with the `admin_role` role; user management is available only to them regardless of the permission matrix |
| Auto-login token | a random string in the browser cookie that lets the user sign in without a password |
| Attempt lockout | a temporary block of sign-in for a login after a series of failed attempts |
| Manual block | a permanent block of a user's sign-in by an administrator until the administrator lifts it |
| Event | a notification from the package to the application about a significant action (failed sign-in, block, deletion, etc.) |

# System overview

```
 Browser                      Application server (R, Shiny)                    Database
 -------                      -----------------------------                    --------
 sign-in form --password-->  aa_auth_server()  --check-->  users            (hash, role, blocked)
 cookie with token ------->  auto-login        --lookup->  auth_sessions    (sha256 of token, expiry, revoked)
 tabs and buttons -------->  aa_can()/aa_require() in each  login_attempts  (login, success, time)
                             application handler
 "Access" tab ------------>  aa_users_server()  --changes--> users, auth_sessions, login_attempts
                             `-> on_event(...) --> the application writes its own log
```

## Data

The package owns seven tables. Their names and columns are fixed, so existing compatible databases can be connected without migrating data.

* **`users`**: `id` (auto-increment), `login` (unique, not empty), `password` (hash), `role`, `blocked` (0 or 1, default 0), `must_change` (0 or 1, default 0: an administrator set the password and the user must change it at sign-in).
  The columns `totp_secret` (the TOTP secret **in encrypted form**), `totp_enabled` (0 or 1) and `totp_last_step` (the last accepted time step, protection against code reuse) appeared in version 0.5.0.
  The `email` column (since version 0.4.0) stores the password recovery address in lower case; it allows NULL, and uniqueness applies only to addresses that are set.
* **`auth_sessions`**: `id`, `user_login`, `token_hash`, `created_at`, `expires_at`, `revoked`. The database stores the **sha256 of the token**; the token itself exists only in the browser cookie. Stealing the database does not yield usable tokens.
* **`login_attempts`**: `id`, `login` (the exact login as typed, case-sensitive, truncated to `login_max` characters), `success`, `attempted_at` (UTC). Index on `(login, attempted_at)`.
* **`password_resets`**: `id`, `user_login`, `token_hash`, `created_at`, `expires_at`, `used`. The database stores the **sha256 of the token** from the email; the token itself exists only in the email. The token is single-use and lives for `reset_ttl_minutes` minutes (60 by default).
* **`totp_recovery`**: `id`, `user_login`, `code_hash`, `used`, `created_at`. The database stores the **sha256 of the backup code**; the codes themselves are shown to the user once, when 2FA is enabled.
* **`oauth_states`** (since version 0.7.0): parameters of the sign-in with Google (`state_hash` only as sha256, `nonce`, `code_verifier`, `created_at`, `expires_at`, `used`); a record lives for 10 minutes and is used once.
* **`appauth_migrations`**: an internal table of schema migration versions.

## Databases

Table and column names are the same in all supported databases (SQLite, DuckDB, MySQL / MariaDB, PostgreSQL); the differences are collected in a single source file, `R/dialect.R`:

* **Time** is stored as text `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS` in UTC and computed in R (not by database functions), so comparing deadlines works the same everywhere and does not depend on the database server's clock or time zone.
* **Logins, roles and hashes** are compared exactly. In MySQL, where ordinary string comparison is case-insensitive, such columns are created with a binary collation that does not ignore trailing spaces (`utf8mb4_0900_bin`, in MariaDB `utf8mb4_nopad_bin`), so `Alice`, `alice` and `alice ` remain different logins.
* **Single use of tokens** (password reset, Google `state`, 2FA backup codes) is ensured by an atomic `UPDATE ... WHERE used = 0`: of two simultaneous requests only one succeeds. This is exactly why stores without such updates and unique constraints (BigQuery and similar) are not suitable.
* **Migrations** are idempotent. In MySQL and PostgreSQL they run under a lock (`GET_LOCK`, `pg_advisory_xact_lock`) so that several app instances starting at once do not conflict. In MySQL DDL cannot be rolled back, so if a migration is interrupted, a rerun completes what is missing.
* **DuckDB** opens the file from a single process and does not allow altering a table that has an index, so `users` is created with all columns at once.

## Trust boundaries

Everything that comes from the browser is untrusted: in Shiny the client can send **any value of any input**, including a button it does not see in the UI. Therefore:

* the role and the signed-in flag are taken only from the server-side session state set by the package's sign-in code, never from an input;
* every action checks the permission on the server at the start of the handler;
* server modules of tabs are registered only for roles that have the permission for the tab, so other roles have no handlers that could be invoked with a forged request.

# Threat model

## What we protect

Password hashes, auto-login tokens, the user's sign-in state, administration functions (creating and deleting users, changing roles and passwords), and through them any application functions available to roles.

## Who we protect against

1. **An anonymous attacker on the network**: guesses passwords, forges requests to the server, tries to sign in without a password.
2. **An authenticated user with low privileges** (`viewer`, `user`): tries to perform actions they are not allowed (privilege escalation, user management, access to other people's data).
3. **Someone who obtained a copy of the database or a backup**: tries to recover passwords and use tokens.
4. **Someone who intercepts traffic** (when HTTPS is absent).
5. **Operator mistakes**: deleting or blocking the last administrator, leaving default passwords.

## Threats and mitigations

| Threat | Mitigation | Residual risk |
|---|---|---|
| SQL injection | All package SQL is parameterised; values from the UI are never substituted into the query text | The application's own SQL is not covered by the package |
| Theft of passwords from the database | Passwords are stored only as scrypt hashes (the `sodium` package) with a per-password salt; a plain-text password in the database is impossible | Weak passwords can be guessed offline; database encryption is not provided |
| Password guessing | Login lockout after N failures within a window, a global limit of failures per minute across all logins | Lockout is per login, not per IP: someone can deliberately lock another person's login |
| Login enumeration | The same message for existing and non-existing logins, response time equalised by a dummy hash check, lockout is counted for non-existing logins too | The different message for a manually blocked account is shown only to someone who knows the correct password |
| Sign-in without a password | There are no fallback sign-in paths: the password is checked only against the hash, there is no plain-text comparison | |
| Forged Shiny requests (calling actions without the required role) | A server-side permission check in every handler, module registration by permission, the role only from server-side state | The application must itself call the checks in its handlers |
| Privilege escalation through user management | User management is available only to the administrator role regardless of the permission matrix; the validity of a role is checked on the server | |
| Theft of the auto-login token | The database holds only the sha256 of the token, the token is random (32 bytes), its lifetime is limited, tokens are revoked on block, password change and user deletion; by default the cookie is written by the server with `HttpOnly` through a short-lived encrypted one-time ticket, so JavaScript never sees the token | `cookie_mode = "legacy"` writes the cookie from JavaScript and allows token theft through XSS; even with `HttpOnly`, XSS can act in the current session |
| Interception of the token on the network | The cookie is written with `SameSite=Lax`, and on HTTPS also with `Secure` (the package does this itself); HTTPS is provided by the application (see the section on application responsibility) | Without HTTPS the token and password travel in plain text |
| Use of someone else's cookie after a user is deleted and a new one is created with the same login | Deleting a user deletes their tokens and failed attempts | |
| The session of a blocked or deleted user keeps working | The live session is checked every 30 seconds and a forced sign-out follows; auto-login for such users is impossible | A window of up to 30 seconds between the block and closing an already open session |
| Race when creating the first administrator | Creation with a single "insert if the table is empty" SQL statement; of two simultaneous sessions only one succeeds | The administrator creation dialog is available to anyone who opens the app on an empty database, so the app should not be exposed externally before the administrator is created |
| Loss of access to the application | You cannot delete or block yourself or the last active administrator | |
| Enumeration of logins and addresses via the "Forgot your password?" form | The on-screen response is always the same (user found or not, has an address or not, blocked or not); the reason goes only into the `password_reset_requested` event | Response time may depend on whether an email was sent: if this matters, move sending the email in `send_reset` to the background |
| Mass-mailing recovery emails to other users | No more than `reset_max_per_hour` emails per user per hour and `reset_max_per_minute` emails per minute overall | A user can be "spammed" up to the limit |
| Reuse and guessing of the token from the email | A 256-bit token, only the hash in the database, single use, limited lifetime, a new request invalidates earlier links, a weak password does not consume the token, a race between two requests is resolved by atomically claiming the token | |
| Leak of the link from the email through the address bar | The module immediately removes `reset` from the page address; the link is single-use and short-lived | The address with the token stays in proxy logs while the link is valid: the key in them is no better protected than the logs themselves |
| Guessing the second-factor code | The code is checked only after the correct password; a wrong code counts as a failed sign-in attempt, and the login is blocked under the same rules as for password guessing; a successful password is not recorded until the correct code, so it does not reset the counter | A window of 3 time steps of 30 seconds: with the default limit (5 failures in 15 minutes) the chance of guessing the code within one lockout is about 15 in a million |
| Reuse of an observed code | The accepted time step is stored with an atomic query; the same code and all earlier steps no longer pass | |
| Theft of the database file | The TOTP secret is encrypted (sodium) with the `totp_key` key, which is stored outside the database; passwords and backup codes are stored only as hashes | Someone who steals both the database and the key obtains the secrets: keep the key separate from the database and its backups |
| Loss of the phone | 10 backup codes (single use), and also a 2FA reset by an administrator in the user card (the user's sessions are ended) | Backup codes should be stored separately from the phone |
| Default passwords (`root/root`, login = password) | The package creates no default users; the hygiene function finds accounts with obviously weak passwords | The check must be run and the passwords changed |

## Outside the threat model

Single sign-on, protection of the user's mailbox and of the device with the authenticator app (whoever receives the email can change the password), protection against malicious code on the user's computer, physical access to the server, attacks at the network and infrastructure level.

# Flows

## Password sign-in

1. The **global limit** of failed attempts in the last minute across all logins is checked. If exceeded, sign-in is temporarily closed for everyone and the password is not checked.
2. The **login lockout** is checked. The login is treated **exactly**, as in the sign-in itself: case and spaces are preserved (truncation only to `login_max` characters), so `Alice` and `alice` are different logins with separate counters. If the login is blocked, the password is not checked and the attempt is not recorded, so the lockout is not extended.
3. The **password check** runs. The user is looked up by login and the password is verified against the hash. If the user does not exist, the check is performed against a dummy hash so that the response time does not reveal whether the login exists.
4. If the password is correct but the account is **manually blocked**, a message about this is shown, the attempt is counted neither as successful nor as failed, and no token is issued.
5. Otherwise the result of the attempt is recorded. A successful sign-in **resets** the failure counter (by the monotonic record number, not by time, because time is stored with one-second precision). A failure after which the limit has accumulated puts the login into lockout and reports it.
6. If the user has `must_change` set (an administrator set the password), the **change password form** is shown instead of signing in: no token is issued and the user does not get into the app until they set their own password. The form asks only for the new password: the temporary password is known to the administrator, so confirming it would not prove ownership. The same form is used after a Google sign-in when `must_change` is set; the old password is not needed there either. The old password does not work after the change.
7. On success an **auto-login token** is issued: 32 random bytes encoded in base64, sha256 stored in the database, a default lifetime of 30 days. With `cookie_mode = "httponly"` the server creates a short-lived encrypted one-time ticket, the browser exchanges it at a same-origin endpoint, and the endpoint sets the cookie with `HttpOnly`; with `cookie_mode = "legacy"` the cookie is written from JavaScript.

Parameters (defaults): 5 failures within a 15-minute window lock the login for 15 minutes from the last failure, a global limit of 30 failures per minute, a password of 6 to 128 characters (the restriction applies only to new and reset passwords; existing ones are not affected).

## First run

If the `users` table has no records, the administrator creation form is shown instead of the sign-in form. The user is **always created with the administrator role** by a single SQL statement that inserts the record only if the table is empty. After creation the user is signed in.

## Cookie auto-login

The browser sends the token, the server computes its sha256 and looks up the record: the token is not revoked, not expired, and the user exists, is not blocked and is not required to change the password. Blocked and deleted users, as well as users required to change their password, do not sign in by cookie. Auto-login is disabled with an application setting (`autologin = FALSE`).

With `cookie_mode = "httponly"` (the default) the server reads the cookie from the HTTP request; in `cookie_mode = "legacy"` JavaScript sends it to a module input. The Google OAuth `state` cookie is written and cleared by the same mechanism. Cookies carry `SameSite` and `Path` from the settings (`cookie_samesite`, `cookie_path`), `Secure` is chosen from the request unless `cookie_secure` is set explicitly, and no cookie is issued when `autologin = FALSE` or `password_login = FALSE` with no Google sign-in.

## Sign-out and forced sign-out

Sign-out revokes the browser token, records an event, clears the cookie, resets the session state and **reloads the page**, so that no handlers registered for the previous user are left in the session. Every 30 seconds ([aa_session_guard()]) it is checked that the user exists, is not blocked, their role in the database has not changed and the token of this session is not revoked; otherwise a forced sign-out is performed with a reason (`deleted`, `blocked`, `role_changed`, `token_revoked`). The guard also deletes stale sign-in attempts and tokens once an hour.

## Changing your own password

The user confirms the current password and sets a new one (under the rules from the settings, different from the current one). The tokens of other sessions are revoked, the token of the current one stays, and `must_change` is cleared. A wrong current password, a weak password or the same password are rejected with a clear message.

## Password recovery by email

Enabled with the `reset_enabled = TRUE` setting; it requires the `send_reset(email, link, login)` function and the application address `reset_base_url`. The user must have an email set (an administrator sets it in the user card or when creating the user).

1. On the sign-in form the "Forgot your password?" link opens a "Login or email" field. The user enters a value and **always sees the same response**.
2. The package looks up the user (the login is compared exactly, the address case-insensitively). No email is sent if the user does not exist, has no address, is blocked, or a limit is exceeded (`reset_max_per_hour` per user, `reset_max_per_minute` overall). The reason is recorded in the `password_reset_requested` event.
3. Otherwise a random token (32 bytes) is created, its sha256 and lifetime are written to the database, the user's earlier unused links are invalidated, and the application function sends an email with the link `<reset_base_url>/?reset=<token>`. If sending fails, the token is invalidated.
4. On opening the link the sign-in module reads the `reset` parameter, **removes it from the address bar** and, if the token is valid (exists, unused, not expired, the user is not blocked), shows the new password form. Otherwise a message and the regular sign-in form are shown (event `password_reset_failed`).
5. The new password is checked against the rules from the settings. A weak password in `reject` mode is rejected and **does not consume the token**. Then the token is claimed with an atomic query (of two simultaneous requests only one succeeds), the password is written, all auto-login tokens are revoked, the other links are invalidated, and the attempt lockout and the must-change requirement are cleared. Event `password_reset_done`.
6. There is no automatic sign-in after the change: the user signs in with the new password in the usual way.

An administrator who resets a password manually, or a user who changes their own password, also invalidates unused links.

## Two-factor authentication

Enabled with the `totp_enabled = TRUE` setting; it requires an encryption key `totp_key` (a string of at least 16 characters, kept outside the database and outside the repository). The protection is **optional**: each user enables it themselves in the account block (`aa_totp_ui()` and `aa_totp_server()`), and whoever has it enabled enters a code at sign-in.

**Setup.** A button creates a secret (160 bits) and stores it encrypted; 2FA is not yet on. The user scans the QR code (if the optional `qrcode` package is installed) or enters the key manually. After a correct code from the app the protection is enabled, the user is shown 10 backup codes once, and their other sessions are ended.

**Sign-in.**

1. The password is checked as usual. If the user has 2FA enabled, **no auto-login token is issued and the successful sign-in attempt is not recorded**: otherwise it would reset the failure counter and the code could be guessed indefinitely.
2. The code form is shown. Before every check the shared sign-in guard (`aa_login_gate()`) is called: a blocked login or the global limit closes the form.
3. A code from the app (6 digits) or a backup code is accepted. A code from the app passes once (the time step is remembered), within a window of +/-`totp_window` steps (1 by default). A backup code is single-use.
4. A wrong code is recorded as a failed attempt (event `totp_failed`). When the login gets blocked, the code form is closed and the user has to start again from the password once the lockout ends.
5. After a correct code a successful attempt is recorded, a token is issued, and then (if the password is temporary) the change password form is shown.

Signing in by auto-login cookie does not ask for the second factor: the cookie was issued after it was passed and is valid for `session_days` days, effectively a "trusted device". Password recovery by email does not bypass 2FA: after the password change the code is still required.

**Disabling.** The user needs the password and a code (or a backup code); otherwise someone who took over another person's open session could remove the protection. The code is checked only when the password is correct, so a third party's attempt does not consume backup codes. Wrong attempts count as failed sign-in attempts.

**Loss of the phone.** Backup codes, or a 2FA reset by an administrator in the user card (the secret and backup codes are erased, the user's sessions are ended, event `totp_reset`).

## Permission checks

* The permission source returns the user's permissions; by default it is built from the "permission -> roles" matrix. An unknown permission means denial (fail-closed behaviour).
* The check in a handler takes the role from the server-side state. On denial the action is aborted, the user gets a notification, and the `access_denied` event is reported to the package.
* Registration of tab server modules is performed only for roles that have the permission for the tab.

## User management (administrator only)

* **Adding**: the login and password are checked against the rules; the user is created with a valid role.
* **Changing the role**: the validity of the role is checked on the server, and the administrator role cannot be removed from the last active administrator.
* **2FA reset**: the administrator erases the user's secret and backup codes and ends their sessions (event `totp_reset`).
* **Email**: the administrator sets, changes or removes the password recovery address (format and uniqueness are checked on the server), event `email_changed`.
* **Password reset**: a new hash is written, **all tokens of the user are revoked** (open sessions will be ended by the guard), and `must_change` is set by default.
* **End all sessions**: all tokens of the user are revoked; the guard ends their open sessions.
* **Manual block**: the `blocked` flag is set and **all tokens are revoked**. You cannot block yourself or the last active administrator.
* **Lifting the attempt lockout**: the login's failed attempts are deleted. Unblocking manually lifts it as well.
* **Deletion**: you cannot delete yourself or the last active administrator; together with the record, the tokens, password recovery links, 2FA backup codes and failed attempts are deleted.

## Application start

At start the application calls the schema preparation: missing tables and columns are created, migrations are applied, and stale data is removed (attempts older than a day, tokens expired or revoked more than 30 days ago, used and expired password recovery links older than a day). A preparation error does not stop the application: lockout protection does not work if the table is missing, but password sign-in keeps working (see the section on decisions).

# Guarantees

These are the properties the package must preserve across all changes. Each is covered by an automated test.

1. A plain-text password is never accepted or compared; a value in the `password` column that is not a hash does not pass verification.
2. Package SQL contains only parameters; user values are never substituted into the query text.
3. Messages about invalid credentials are the same for existing and non-existing logins.
4. Attempts during a lockout are not recorded and do not extend the lockout.
5. Lockout and sign-in treat the login identically and exactly: a different spelling of the login (case, spaces) does not sign in at all, so it cannot be used to bypass a lockout, and failed attempts under a non-existent spelling do not lock out the real user. The login of a new user cannot match an existing one even up to case.
6. A successful sign-in resets the failure counter regardless of the records having been made within the same second.
7. A blocked or deleted user does not sign in by password or by cookie, and their tokens are invalid.
8. Password reset, blocking and deletion revoke or delete the user's tokens.
9. A new user with a login that previously belonged to another person does not get access via the other person's cookie and does not inherit their lockout.
10. You cannot be left without an active administrator through blocking, deletion or a role change.
11. The first administrator is created only on an empty table, including under simultaneous requests.
12. Migrations are repeatable: a rerun changes nothing, and existing data (users, hashes, tokens) is not modified.
13. An unknown permission means denial.

# Decisions and their reasons

| Decision | Reason | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| scrypt hashing (`sodium::password_store`) | Modern, resistant to brute force on specialised hardware, the hash contains the salt and parameters, available in `sodium` with no external dependencies | Sign-in is slightly slower than with a plain hash; that is the protection |
| The auto-login token is stored as sha256 | A database leak does not reveal working tokens, and the tokens are random and long, so a slow hash is not needed | |
| Lockout by login, not by IP | Behind a reverse proxy the application sees the proxy address, not the client's | Someone can deliberately lock another person's login. Mitigation: a short lockout, event recording, an unlock button for the administrator |
| The login is compared and counted in lockouts exactly (case-sensitive, without lower-casing) | SQLite compares logins the same way, and real data is stored this way: a production database may contain distinct users `alice` and `Alice`; lower-casing would give them a shared counter and let failures against a non-existent `Bob` lock out the real `bob` | A new user cannot be given a login that differs from an existing one only by case; existing pairs are preserved |
| Attempts during a lockout are not recorded | Otherwise a legitimate user extends the lockout and an attacker keeps it up indefinitely | |
| The counter is reset by record number, not by time | Time is stored with one-second precision, and quick events were lost (a bug found by tests) | |
| The lockout check fails open, the password check fails closed | Unavailability of the attempts table must not lock out all users, but the password check is never skipped | If the table could not be created, brute-force protection does not work; the error is written to the application log |
| The cookie is set by a same-origin HTTP handler through a short-lived encrypted one-time ticket | Shiny has no public API for setting cookies, but an internal HTTP handler can accept an opaque ticket and return `Set-Cookie`; only the ticket hash is stored in the database, and JavaScript never sees the token | Requires a handler registration per process and a separate ticket table; `cookie_mode = "legacy"` remains for apps that need the old JavaScript flow |
| Forced sign-out is checked on a timer | Shiny does not receive events from the database other than its own queries | Up to 30 seconds between the block and closing an open session |
| Page reload on sign-out | Otherwise the module handlers of the previous user stay registered in this session | The page is redrawn |
| User management only for the administrator regardless of the permission matrix | Otherwise granting this permission to a role would let it raise its own privileges | The permission for the user management tab cannot be delegated |
| The permission source is plugged in as a function and not hard-wired into the config structure | Applications store permissions differently (YAML, database, per user) | The application is responsible for the correctness of its source |
| A single event hook instead of writing to logs | The package does not impose a log schema, and applications have different ones | The application must implement the hook, otherwise events go nowhere |
| Password recovery is off by default and the email is sent by an application function | Not every application has email and user addresses; the package should not pull in SMTP and sending credentials | The application writes the sending function and is responsible for delivering the email |
| A link with the token in the address rather than a code from the email | No separate code entry form and no need to protect the code against guessing; the token cannot be guessed | `reset_base_url` is needed, and the token is visible in proxy logs until used |
| TOTP is implemented in the package (HMAC-SHA1 from `openssl`, verified against the RFC 4226 and 6238 reference vectors), with no new dependencies | New packages would have to be installed into the shared server library; the algorithm is short and verifiable | Only TOTP is supported (no SMS, push or hardware keys) |
| QR code through the optional `qrcode` package | Does not inflate the mandatory dependencies | Without the package the user enters the key manually |
| The secret is encrypted with the application key (`totp_key`), not hashed | The server must know the secret to verify codes | Losing or replacing the key makes the secrets unreadable: users have to set up 2FA again (an administrator resets it in the user card) |
| The successful sign-in attempt is recorded only after the code | Otherwise the password would reset the failure counter and the code could be guessed without limit | |
| 2FA is optional | Forcing it on for roles requires a "first sign-in without 2FA" scenario and emergency access | Administrators may remain without a second factor if they do not enable it themselves |
| SQLite by default, plus DuckDB, MySQL / MariaDB and PostgreSQL through a dialect layer (`R/dialect.R`) | Most applications use SQLite, and existing databases should connect without migration; the other databases are for applications that already have a server | Time is computed by R and written as UTC text rather than a database type; DDL cannot be rolled back in MySQL; BigQuery is not supported: no unique constraints or atomic updates |

# Known limitations

These limitations are known and accepted. They should be taken into account when assessing an application's risk.

* **Legacy cookie mode**: `cookie_mode = "legacy"` writes the cookie from JavaScript and has no `HttpOnly`, so XSS in the application can steal the token; keep the default `httponly` mode unless an application specifically needs the old behavior. Even with `HttpOnly`, XSS can act in the current session, so the application must not render unchecked HTML.
* **Cookie and HTTPS**: the cookie is written with `SameSite=Lax` by default, and `Secure` is set automatically for HTTPS requests or can be forced with `cookie_secure = TRUE`; without HTTPS the token may travel in plain text, so the application should be published only over HTTPS (see the `deployment` vignette).
* **Lockout by login**: deliberately locking another person's login for the duration of the window is possible, including the administrator's. A spare administrator should exist for this.
* **The password is checked only by length**: no list of forbidden passwords is used.
* **Single sign-on only through Google.** There are no other providers (Microsoft, Okta, SAML). Signing in with Google is equivalent to access to the person's Google account: whoever controls it can sign in to the application, so the organisation (Workspace) protects access to the account. The user must be created in the application in advance, and their email in the database must match the Google address. Changing a user's email in Workspace without updating the address in the application closes their Google sign-in, and handing the address to another person opens the first user's account to them, so addresses must be kept up to date. The two-factor code of the application is not requested when signing in with Google. Two-factor protection is optional and only by TOTP codes: no SMS, push notifications, hardware keys, and no forced enabling for roles.
* **Losing the `totp_key` key** makes the stored secrets unreadable: until an administrator resets 2FA, users with the protection enabled cannot sign in (the code will not match).
* **Server and phone clocks**: the code is tied to time, and a discrepancy larger than the window (30 seconds by default) blocks sign-in; time synchronisation (NTP) is required.
* **The recovery email is a key to the account**: whoever controls the user's mailbox can change their password. Enable recovery only if the email addresses can be trusted; for administrators you can leave the address empty and keep manual reset.
* **Up to 30 seconds** between blocking a user and closing their open session.
* **Only SQLite, DuckDB, MySQL / MariaDB and PostgreSQL are supported.** BigQuery and other analytical stores are not suitable: single-use tokens and protection of the last administrator require atomic updates and unique constraints. DuckDB opens the file from a single process. In MySQL logins are compared exactly only in columns created by the package (binary collation): a `users` table created manually with an ordinary collation must be recreated.
* **No independent security audit has been performed**: the properties are confirmed by automated tests and by fixing the bugs found, but not by an external specialist.

# Application responsibility

The package is secure only when used correctly. The application must:

1. **Call the permission check at the start of every action handler** and register tab server modules only for roles with the permission for the tab. Hiding buttons in the UI is not protection.
2. **Validate the inputs of its own functions**: compare file, service and task names against allow-lists, run OS commands without string concatenation, and do not render unchecked HTML.
3. **Close the database connection when the session ends** (`session$onSessionEnded`), otherwise connections accumulate, and on Windows the database file cannot be renamed or deleted while the R process is alive.
4. **Use HTTPS** (the `Secure` cookie flag on HTTPS and `SameSite=Lax` are set by the package itself). The application must not be reachable directly without a proxy that provides HTTPS.
5. **Not keep `config.yaml`, the database and secrets in the repository and images**, and not serve the whole database through the UI (it holds the tables of users, tokens and sign-in attempts).
6. **Implement the event hook** and persist sign-in, lockout and access-denied events so that guessing attempts are visible.
7. **Not create default users**, and change the passwords found by the weak-account check.
8. **Have a spare administrator** in case of deliberate lockout.
9. **Keep the `totp_key` key outside the database and the repository** (an environment variable) and not lose it: without it the TOTP secrets cannot be decrypted. Keep database backups separate from the key.

# Compatibility and migrations

When the package is connected, versioned migrations run: missing tables and columns are created, existing data is not modified, and a rerun changes nothing. An older schema is recognised too (for example a `users` table without the `id` column or without `blocked`). Passwords that were stored in plain text are converted to hashes by a separate one-time function with a database backup and a transaction; until this step, signing in with such passwords is impossible, because the package does not accept plain-text passwords.

# Lessons from bugs found

The package was created from an application whose authentication had to be fixed during an audit. Each problem found became a requirement for the package and a test.

| What was found | Lesson and protection in the package |
|---|---|
| SQL was built by string concatenation, sign-in without a password via `' OR '1'='1` | Only parameterised queries |
| Passwords in plain text in the database, in backups, in git history and on a network drive | Only hashes, a migration with a backup, documentation about copies and history |
| A button hidden in the UI was executed by a forged request, and the server module of the command line was reachable without signing in | Permission checks in every handler, module registration by permission |
| A user could delete themselves and the last administrator | Unified validity checks for blocking and deletion |
| A new user with the same login signed in by the previous owner's cookie | Deleting tokens and attempts together with the user |
| The attempt counter was not reset if a success and new failures fell within the same second | Reset by record number |
| The database connection was not closed when the session ended and kept the file locked | Closing connections in the application, a regression test on renaming the database file |
| A new variant of the default settings lost a permission that was present in the hand-edited working config, and the button disappeared for everyone | A test "all permissions used by the code are in the default settings", appending missing settings without overwriting existing ones |
| An inline table row colour was not displayed because the app theme overrides it | Styling rows with CSS classes and checking in a real browser, not only against the table description |

# Document history

* The users table shows whether a password recovery email is set, whether 2FA is enabled, and how many active auto-logins the user has (version 0.6.0, `aa_active_autologins()`). An auto-login is a token in a cookie: the number shows on how many devices sign-in is remembered, not how many tabs are open.
* Added TOTP two-factor authentication (version 0.5.0): `totp_*` columns in `users`, the `totp_recovery` table (migration 8), the `aa_totp_*` module, the `totp_*` events and `recovery_code_used`.
* Added password recovery by email (version 0.4.0): the `users.email` column, the `password_resets` table (migration 7), single-use links, limits, the `password_reset_*` events and `email_changed`.
* Added: changing your own password, mandatory password change for passwords set by an administrator (`must_change`), ending all of a user's sessions, session token checking by the guard, periodic cleanup of stale records, sign-in on Enter.
* First version: a description of the intended behaviour of the package before code was extracted from the application. The document is refined as the package is implemented and verified.
